clue.text: Clean away second part of litter

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, a second
a pup is one of a litter of young dogs

explanation.surface: Someone tidying up is told to clear away the second lot of rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of litter' looks like a piece of rubbish; it is one of the young born together to a dog.
explanation.definitionFit: To mop up is a phrasal verb for finishing off cleaning, wiping or clearing the last remnants.

clue.text: Florentine family with name, to Italian, for ill-treatment?

blocks.note: the Medici were the ruling family of Renaissance Florence
N is the abbreviation for name
al is Italian for 'to the'

explanation.surface: A cruel Florentine dynasty turns its name over to Italy as punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: Ill-treatment hints at cruelty but means treating the ill, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Medicinal describes remedies used to treat illness, which is what treatment for the sick means.

clue.text: President leading a dance

blocks.note: James K. Polk was the eleventh US president
taken as written

explanation.surface: A head of state opens the ball by leading the first dance.
explanation.definitionFit: The polka is a lively Bohemian couple dance in two-four time, one kind of dance.

clue.text: Girl's on show in building here in Paris

indicators.note: something on show in a place is displayed inside it

blocks.note: a pile is a large imposing building
gal is a colloquial word for a girl

explanation.surface: A woman is performing in a theatre somewhere in Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: Pigalle is the Paris district of nightclubs and the Moulin Rouge, which suits a girl on show.
explanation.definitionFit: Pigalle is a district of northern Paris, so it is a place found in the French capital.

clue.text: Boss shy? That can be an advantage at first

definitions.text: That can be an advantage at first

blocks.note: the head is the boss or chief
to shy, as a horse does, is to start or jump in alarm

explanation.surface: A timid manager wonders whether shyness could be a benefit early on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shy' reads as timid, but here it is the verb for a horse flinching, as in start.
explanation.definitionFit: A head start is a lead given at the beginning of a race, an early edge over rivals.

clue.text: Make sharp with stone, but not too sharp

blocks.note: to hone a blade is to sharpen it
st is the abbreviation for stone, the British weight; 'with' adds it on

explanation.surface: Sharpen a knife on a whetstone, but don't overdo the edge.
explanation.walkthrough: Sharp here also means sharp practice: someone not too sharp is not a cheat. A stone is a British weight of fourteen pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who avoids sharp, crafty dealing is truthful and fair, the opposite of a swindler.

clue.text: Mixed race man, one found in the melting-pot?

definitions.note: adjectival phrase, as an adjective describing a person from the melting-pot nation

indicators.note: mixed means the letters are blended together into a new order

blocks.note: letters taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A man of mixed race is the sort of person found in a melting-pot society.
explanation.walkthrough: The United States is often called the melting-pot, where many peoples blend.
explanation.definitionFit: The USA is famously described as a melting-pot of immigrant peoples, so its citizens are found there.

clue.text: Covered in stones hard to put in by oneself

indicators.note: to put in means one letter is placed inside the other word

blocks.note: singly means alone, one by oneself
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Pebbles are difficult to lay by yourself on a stony path.
explanation.definitionFit: Shingle is a mass of small rounded pebbles, so a shingly beach is strewn with them.

clue.text: A neck and a leg muddy? Get sponge

indicators.note: muddy as a verb means to stir up and confuse, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: letters of A, neck, a and leg; 'and' only joins

explanation.surface: Someone with a dirty neck and leg is told to fetch a sponge and wash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sponge' looks like a bath sponge for the muddy body; it is the cake.
explanation.definitionFit: Angel cake is a light, airy sponge made with egg whites, a kind of sponge cake.

clue.text: Part of habitat typically cheap and nasty

indicators.note: part of means only a stretch of the following words is taken

blocks.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Some animal habitat is usually shabby and run-down.
explanation.definitionFit: Tatty is a British informal word for shabby, worn out and of poor quality.

clue.text: Vehicle application

blocks.note: first meaning: a French public stagecoach
second meaning: steady, careful effort at work

explanation.walkthrough: The two words look like a form for a car licence; they are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both an old continental stagecoach and the quality of persistent hard work.

clue.text: Home secured in highly valued block

blocks.note: to be in is to be at home
secured as in obtained

explanation.surface: A house is bought cheaply as part of a prized building block.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingot is a cast bar of gold or silver, a precious metal block of great worth.

clue.text: English clerk, say, turned into author

indicators.note: turned into says the words are transformed, their letters made into something new

blocks.note: all three words are used as letters

explanation.surface: An English office clerk, for example, became a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Kingsley was the Victorian author of The Water-Babies and Westward Ho!
explanation.definitionFit: Kingsley was a Victorian novelist and clergyman, so he is an example of a writer.

clue.text: Points — six of them

blocks.note: six points of the compass in a row: north, east, south, south, east, south

explanation.surface: A navigator counts off a list of six compass bearings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Points' does double duty: nesses are headlands, and the word itself is spelt from six compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: A ness is a headland or promontory jutting into the sea, a point of land on a coast.

clue.text: They're responsible for vital points in line management

definitions.text: They're responsible for vital points in line management

blocks.clueFragment: They're responsible for vital points in line management
blocks.note: surface reading: managers who make the key points to the people under them in the line of command
setter's reading: the points are railway switches and the line is a railway track, run by staff in signal boxes

explanation.walkthrough: Line management sounds like office hierarchy; it is the railway line, where points switch trains between tracks.
explanation.definitionFit: Railway signal-box workers operate the signals and points that keep trains on the right track safely.

clue.text: Shakespearean adaptor's inseparable companions in nursery

blocks.note: first meaning: co-writer with her brother Charles of Tales from Shakespeare, retelling the plays for children
second meaning: the girl and her pet in the nursery rhyme, where the pet followed her to school

explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words, the answer is the rhyme's girl and her little pet, who went everywhere together.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery rhyme pair never parted, and the writer of that name adapted Shakespeare's plays into prose tales for children.

clue.text: Bowled with exhilaration, and not before time

blocks.note: B is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for bowled
with exhilaration is elatedly, in a thrilled way

explanation.surface: A cricketer bowled with joy and, at last, on time.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'exhilaration' fragment takes the 'with' before it to make the adverb.
explanation.definitionFit: Belatedly means late, coming after the expected moment, which is what not before time says.

clue.text: President replacing leader of military unit with next character

indicators.note: replacing the leader means the first letter is swapped for another

blocks.note: a garrison is a body of troops stationed in a town
the letter after G in the alphabet

explanation.surface: A president swaps the commander of an army unit for the next in line.
explanation.walkthrough: William Henry Harrison and Benjamin Harrison were both US presidents.
explanation.definitionFit: Two US heads of state bore the surname Harrison, the ninth and twenty-third.

clue.text: Soldier, in places, an absolutely rational person

indicators.note: in says the soldier is set inside the word for places

blocks.note: loci is the Latin plural for places
a GI is an American soldier
taken as written

explanation.surface: A soldier, here and there, is a thoroughly sensible person.
explanation.definitionFit: A logician studies formal reasoning, so is a person given wholly to rational argument.

clue.text: Firm and practice share accommodation

blocks.note: Co is the abbreviation for company, a firm
a habit is a regular practice

explanation.surface: A company and a professional practice decide to share offices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' and 'practice' suggest a law firm sharing premises.
explanation.definitionFit: To cohabit is to live together under one roof, usually as an unmarried couple.

clue.text: Poet in circle we joined in the fifties

indicators.note: in places the circle and the pronoun inside the string of fifties, after the first

blocks.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, so a run of fifties gives a string of Ls
a circle is the shape of the letter O
taken as written

explanation.surface: A poet joined a literary circle back in the 1950s.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a decade; it is really two Roman fifties. Robert Lowell was the American poet of Life Studies.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Lowell and James Russell Lowell were both American writers of verse.

clue.text: Heavy, heavy blow's nothing to us

blocks.note: a oner is British slang for a single heavy blow
O looks like zero, nothing
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tough guy shrugs off a heavy punch as nothing to worry about.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'heavy' hides the split: the first is the definition, the second starts the wordplay. A oner is a knockout blow in British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: An onerous task is burdensome and weighty, so heavy in the figurative sense.

clue.text: Group of soldiers surrounding university college

indicators.note: surrounding means one word goes round the other

blocks.note: a corps is an army formation
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Troops surround a university campus.
explanation.walkthrough: Corpus Christi is a college at both Oxford and Cambridge, known for short as Corpus.
explanation.definitionFit: Corpus is the usual short name for Corpus Christi, a constituent college at Oxford and Cambridge.

clue.text: Don includes article warning players, with prediction important for sport

indicators.note: includes means one word holds another within it

blocks.note: to don clothes is to wear them
the definite article
fore is the golfer's warning shout
the cast are the players in a show

explanation.surface: A university don writes a piece cautioning players, making a key sporting forecast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' looks like an Oxbridge tutor but is the verb to put on.
explanation.definitionFit: A forecast of rain or sun decides whether a match goes ahead, so it matters greatly to sport.

clue.text: Extras provided by wife — mostly, that is

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for wife
id est is the Latin for that is

explanation.surface: Extra help comes mainly from the wife, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: Wides are extras in cricket: runs added when a ball is bowled out of the batsman's reach.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a wide is a delivery out of reach, scoring an extra run not credited to a batter.

clue.text: Play opener in test, bursting with fitness

indicators.note: the opener in a word is its first letter
bursting means breaking apart, so the letters fly out of order

blocks.note: letters taken as written
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A batsman opening a Test innings bursts with fitness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play opener' looks like a single phrase; the anagram fodder is play plus the opener in test.
explanation.definitionFit: Aptly means suitably or appropriately, and fitness here is the sense of being suitable.

clue.text: After protest, bishop is leaving the service

blocks.note: a demo is a protest march
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: Following a protest, a bishop quits the church service.
explanation.walkthrough: The service sounds churchy beside the bishop; it is military service. Demob is British for discharge from the forces.
explanation.definitionFit: Demob is a colloquial verb for being discharged from the armed forces at the end of a war.

clue.text: Played around at university, being financially maintained

indicators.note: around means one word wraps itself about the other

blocks.note: sported means played or frolicked
to be up is to be in residence at university

explanation.surface: A student fooled about at college while living on an allowance.
explanation.definitionFit: To be supported is to be kept or provided for with money by someone else.

clue.text: These short pieces, my boy, ain't difficult as all that

indicators.note: something difficult is awkward and contorted, so these letters are twisted out of order

blocks.note: a son is one's boy
letters taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A parent reassures a son that these little practice pieces are not that hard.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonatina is a short, simple sonata, often given to piano learners as an exercise.

clue.text: Early English author succeeded, at first, in devious way

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for succeeded in family trees
John Lyly was an Elizabethan writer, author of Euphues

explanation.surface: An Elizabethan writer got ahead early by underhand means.
explanation.definitionFit: Slyly is the adverb for acting in a cunning, sneaky or deceitful manner.
